The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. Her father had built it the year she was born, with a through-stone every yard. What caused the collapse was the stream. After the October rains it jumped its bank and ran along the foot of the wall for three days, washing away the footing until the face folded into the water.

Dell Haskett drove up from the fencing yard in Orley with wire in his truck and a cost she could meet, and as he talked he kept glancing at the sky to the north. His fence posts would stand well up the slope from the stream and hold Maren's ram, he said, but she had a fortnight before the frost. "After that, nobody digs a post hole up here until March." The geese had been going over all week, and the air already smelled of snow. Maren said she would make her choice by Sunday.

On Sunday she brought out her father's old notebook, with a sketch of every stone in that stretch, and handed Haskett's card back to him at the gate. I joined her that afternoon. The only flat ground near the gap was the end of the village football pitch, so we sorted the stones there, hauled up from the stream bed by the tractor, and laid them out in his order.

Snow stopped us four weekends running, and by March the gap was still one capstone short. Maren set the last one just as Haskett's truck slowed on the road below, and he leaned out to call that she could have saved herself a winter. "You tried to rush me with your fortnight, and I want you off my road," she called down, and turned her back on the truck.

It was the hardest winter in ten years. At first I thought we would give up by Christmas, and some mornings I learned more about cold than about stone. But we kept on, a few stones at a time, through sleet and frozen wind, and the wall stood whole before the ground thawed.

In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Half the posts had rotted to stumps, and the commissioners wanted to know whether Rudd's line was still true.

Varne spent his first week in the punt with his chainman, Jonah Pell, poling the creek and walking the length of the sea wall before he drove a single stake. Rudd's posts ran along the foot of the wall, where the marsh began, a dozen of them still sound, and the reed-cutters swore every one had crept seaward.

For his fixed point he chose the iron weathercock of Sallow church, the one mark visible from every channel of the delta, and he measured from it to each sound post while the sexton's horse, bred for draft, hauled his stakes along the wall. Every post stood within an inch of where Rudd's old field book put it, and Varne drove his own stakes along the foot of the sea wall beside them.

The last stake went in at Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel, and a grey heron was standing on the very spot. Pell asked whether he should chase the bird off and set the stake. Varne laughed. "Let him finish his fishing first, Jonah, since he was surveying this point long before either of us."

The commissioners entered Varne's map, the work of a single season, in the county book as proof of Rudd's line and had the rotted posts renewed in oak in their old holes. His survey had shown that Rudd's line was right all along, though the reed-cutters still carried their quarrel to the courts.

passage:
When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, telephoned Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street and keeps its piano as it was in the early years, that night to ask which Saturday was free.

Brask telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere, who came the next week. The archivist found the reel sound and supple, and Ines, holding a frame to the window, was the first to recognize the street and place it in town: the striped awning of the bakery where she had once worked. Colm read out a letter from a collector in the city, a smooth pitch that promised a fair price and a cold vault.

Halloway wanted the original locked in the archive before it was run anywhere; a reel that old, she said, belonged where it could be kept cold. Colm wanted the town to see it first, on the Lantern’s screen, where it would have played a century ago. They argued across the lobby for an hour while Brask swept around them.

The archive made the copy after a short delay, and Brask paid for it from the Lantern’s takings. Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist, who has played for its silent nights since she was a girl, worked out a fair-day march for it, and Brask put up posters promising a fair.

But when the copy was screened at the Lantern in October, the oldest people in the house began to murmur, and the town discovered what the reel really showed. The crowd on Ferry Street was carrying chairs through water a foot deep: it was the morning after the great flood, filed in the wrong tin. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She said she would, but only after he took down every poster in Carrow, because it was wrong to keep selling tickets to a fair the reel had never shown.
